definition: The riders a ride could serve per hour if every seat were filled and every dispatch left on time.
The hourly rider count a ride actually achieves after empty seats, slow loads and stoppages.
The time between one vehicle leaving the station and the next one leaving.
The platform position that sorts parties into numbered rows before the gates open.
The average number of people in a queue equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each spends there.
Demand divided by capacity; as it nears 100 percent, queues grow very quickly.
The estimated wait a park shows on the sign and in its app, usually rounded upward.
A card handed to a guest entering a queue and collected at the merge to measure the real wait.
The share of scheduled operating time during which a ride is actually open to guests.
The average running time between stoppages of a ride.
The controlled release of guests from a holding line into the park at opening.
The surge of guests arriving at nearby rides the moment a parade or show ends.
A ticket handed out when a ride breaks down that lets the guest come back later without queueing.
Inspecting and replacing parts on a schedule set by hours or cycles, before they fail.
Checking metal parts for hidden cracks with methods such as ultrasound or magnetic particles that do not damage them.
A planned closure in which a ride's trains, structure, controls or scenes are renewed.
A temporary change of props, lighting and audio that gives a ride a seasonal story without altering the hardware.
The point at which a part or controller is no longer made and must be reverse-engineered or redesigned.
Money spent on long-lived assets such as new rides, lands and hotels, as opposed to daily running costs.
The share of people in a market area expected to visit a park in a year.
Ticket prices that vary by calendar date to push demand toward quieter days.
Revenue divided by attendance; the average amount each guest visit brings in.
The number of days or nights a visiting party spends at a resort.
The quieter weeks on either side of a park's peak, often filled with ticketed events.
A short survey interview with guests as they leave the park.
Pine and Gilmore's name for an economy where memorable experiences, not goods or services, carry the most value.
